claims.claim: Closed-loop community-health-worker (CHW) → nurse → provider referral coordination (three-tier care coordination with every referral tracked to completion, as run by Mi Salud in rural Washington) is nationally applicable in the USA.

rationale.label: (a) Supported by national evidence?
rationale.text: [SUPPORTED] CHW interventions have strong national evidence, including randomized trials (IMPaCT: ~$2,500 saved/patient in year 1, 66% of hospital days vs matched controls) and AHRQ's documentation of pay-for-performance closed-loop models. The closed-loop referral concept itself is an established quality-improvement framework (AHRQ care-coordination literature; peer-reviewed work on closed-loop social-care referrals). Evidence specifically combining all three tiers (CHW → nurse → telehealth provider with loop closure) in US rural settings is thinner but the components are each well-evidenced.

rationale.label: (b) Already practiced nationally?
rationale.text: [PARTIALLY] Named programs practice close variants: Pathways Community HUB / PCHI (CHW "pathways" tracked to completion, nationally certified, used in many communities), IMPaCT (evidence-based CHW program), and closed-loop referral platforms (Unite Us, findhelp, NowPow) used by health systems nationwide — e.g., Sarasota Memorial's Unite Us deployment (Oct 2026) tracks referrals to confirmed completion and reports reduced readmissions; separately, Hawai'i's Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation adopted Findhelp's statewide closed-loop network (Nov 2026), spanning 470+ community organizations. Most recently, the North Carolina State Health Plan (540,000 state-funded members) began a statewide rollout of Infina Connect's ICC closed-loop care-coordination platform through its Preferred Provider Program, targeting full deployment by Jan 1, 2027 (Nov 2026) — closed-loop tracking now reaching a state employee health plan. However, no widely adopted national program combines CHW identification, nurse screening/onboarding, telehealth provider treatment, and mandatory loop closure back to the CHW as a single integrated, tracked workflow — practice is fragmented across these actors.

rationale.label: (c) Feasible under national policy?
rationale.text: [PARTIALLY] Medicare now reimburses CHW-delivered Community Health Integration services (CPT 98160–98162 / G0019, G0022, G0023, G0024, G0322 as of CY2024 PFS), and CHWs may be employed by a community-based organization under general supervision — so the model's billing skeleton exists nationally. The CY2026 PFS final rule (effective Jan 1, 2026) further widened the CHI pathway: MFTs and MHCs can serve as auxiliary personnel, behavioral-health visits can initiate CHI, and the G0019 qualifying-service definition now covers any unmet upstream driver — making it easier for safety-net and behavioral-health practices in rural areas to stand up the CHW tier. But Medicaid CHW coverage is state-by-state (certification, scope, and payment pathways vary widely per NASHP/KFF), and the $50B CMS Rural Health Transformation Program (awards to all 50 states from 2026, ~$200M average first-year) provides grant, not sustained fee-for-service, funding — the Year 2 RHTP awards (Nov 9, 2026) confirmed the program continues at $10B/yr to all 50 states (Washington's Year 2 award: $177.06M, down from $181.26M), now informed by each state's documented implementation progress. Feasibility is real but uneven by state and dependent on braided funding.

rationale.label: (d) Where is the gap? — Mi Salud's integrated loop is the gap
rationale.text:
What is NOT done nationally: (1) systematic tracking of every referral to completion — referral leakage remains high nationally (benchmarks show a large share of referrals never complete); (2) a single accountable workflow spanning CHW identification → nurse screening → telehealth provider → closed-loop return to the CHW — most closed-loop platforms stop at social-service referrals, and most HUB models stop at CHW-to-resource linkage; (3) integrated telehealth provider tier with rural vulnerable-population targeting funded through one coordinated model. This integration is Mi Salud's differentiator; it is nationally applicable in concept but not currently practiced as a unified model nationally.

Key numbers: CHI G0019 national rate ~$80.56/month (60 min), G0022 ~$50.26; IMPaCT RCTs: ~$2,500 saved/patient year 1, 66% of hospital days, 94% NPS; CHW referral completion in community-to-facility literature: 34–97% (median 74%); RHT Program: $50B over 5 years ($10B/yr, FY2026–FY2030), all 50 states, ~$200M average first-year award; Year 2 (FY2027) awards announced Nov 9, 2026, Washington $177.06M (down from $181.26M).

sources.title: Medicare Payment for Community Health Worker Services — CY2024 PFS Final Rule Summary (IMPaCT/CMS)
sources.note: For the first time, Medicare Part B pays for Community Health Integration (CHI) services delivered by CHWs under general supervision of a billing practitioner (CPT 98160–98162 / G0019, G0022, G0023, G0024, G0322), ~$80.56 for G0019 (60 min) and ~$50.26 for G0022 national average. CHWs may work for a community-based organization, so a nonprofit CHW tier can be Medicare-billable nationally.

sources.title: Calendar Year (CY) 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule Fact Sheet (CMS-1832-F)
sources.note: Finalized Oct 31, 2025, effective Jan 1, 2026: expands CHI — Marriage and Family Therapists and Mental Health Counselors join CSWs/RNs as qualifying "certified or trained auxiliary personnel" for G0019; behavioral health visits (psychiatric diagnostic evaluation 90791 and HBAI codes) may now serve as the initiating visit; the G0019 qualifying-service definition broadened from an unmet SDoH need to any unmet upstream driver of the problem addressed. Detail per ICD10monitor analysis (https://medlearn.com/icd10monitor/2026-expansion-for-community-health-integration-coding-g0019/).

sources.title: Sarasota Memorial Demonstrates How Closed-Loop Referrals with Unite Us Reduce Hospital Readmissions (South Florida Hospital News, Oct 21, 2026)
sources.note: Named health-system deployment (Oct 2026): Sarasota Memorial uses Unite Us' closed-loop referral platform to identify non-medical needs during inpatient stays, coordinate referrals to community organizations, and track outcomes to confirm patients received help — with reported reductions in hospital readmissions. Real-world, named-outcome evidence that loop-closure tracking tied to readmission outcomes is now in production at US health systems.

sources.title: State Community Health Worker Policies: 2024–2025 Trends (NASHP)
sources.note: CHW scope-of-practice, certification, and Medicaid payment rules vary state by state; many states now authorize Medicaid CHW reimbursement but there is no uniform national pathway — the main policy constraint on national applicability.

sources.title: State Policies for Expanding Medicaid Coverage of CHW Services (KFF)
sources.note: Medicaid payment for CHW services is authorized in a subset of states and takes differing forms (state plan, waiver, managed-care), confirming significant state variation in feasibility.

sources.title: Community Health Worker Training Program (CHWTP) — HRSA
sources.note: HRSA nationally funds CHW training/outreach for underserved communities, showing federal workforce support exists for the CHW tier of the model.

sources.title: Connecting Those at Risk to Care: Quick Start Guide to the Pathways Community HUB Model (AHRQ)
sources.note: AHRQ documents the Pathways Community HUB — a nationally certified, pay-for- performance care-coordination model in which CHWs work assigned "pathways" that are closed only when the risk factor is resolved — the closest national analogue to Mi Salud's tracked-to-completion loop.

sources.title: Pathways Community HUB Model (PCHI)
sources.note: The PCHI model operates in numerous US communities using CHWs plus a central HUB to remove social barriers, evidencing that closed-loop CHW coordination is already practiced nationally, though not universally.

sources.title: IMPaCT Care — RCT outcomes (summary embedded in PFS Final Rule summary)
sources.note: Multiple RCTs of the IMPaCT CHW program report ~$2,500 saved per patient in year 1, 66% of hospital days vs matched controls, and 94% net promoter score — strong national evidence for CHW-tier impact.

sources.title: A Human-Centered Approach for Designing a Social Care Referral System (PMC11753861)
sources.note: Describes the closed-loop referral concept and commercial platforms (Unite Us, NowPow/CommunityRx, Pieces Iris, Reema Health) that enable bidirectional referral tracking and status feedback in US health systems.

sources.title: Unite Us — Connecting Communities, Data & Care
sources.note: Unite Us operates closed-loop referral networks nationally, showing the referral- tracking infrastructure component is commercially available at national scale.

sources.title: Referral Leakage Benchmark Report 2026 (Linear Health)
sources.note: Referral leakage (referred care never completed) remains a large national problem across specialties — the problem Mi Salud's tracked-to-completion loop targets is widespread and largely unsolved in standard practice.

sources.title: CMS Launches Landmark $50 Billion Rural Health Transformation Program
sources.note: CMS's $50B RHT program (Sept 2025) funds state strategies for rural care-delivery innovation and coordination; ~$200M average first-year awards to all 50 states (announced Dec 29, 2025) create a national financing vehicle for models like this.

sources.title: CMS Announces $50 Billion in Awards to Strengthen Rural Health in All 50 States
sources.note: All 50 states received RHT awards beginning 2026, explicitly supporting "new approaches to coordinating health care services across rural communities.

sources.title: A systematic review of community-to-facility neonatal referral completion rates (PMC4589085)
sources.note: International (mostly LMIC) evidence: CHW-initiated referral completion ranged 34–97% (median 74%), demonstrating both the feasibility and the fallibility of CHW→facility referral loops; US rural-specific data is thinner.

sources.title: Care Coordination — AHRQ
sources.note: AHRQ frames deliberate organizing of patient care activities and timely information sharing among participants as a core quality lever, supporting the coordination concept but without mandating a specific three-tier staffing model.

sources.title: Strengthening Access to CHW Services in New York Through Medicaid (CHCS)
sources.note: The 2024 Medicare CHI launch plus growing state Medicaid CHW pathways are expanding sustainability for CHW services nationally, but coverage design still differs by state.

sources.title: Rural Health Transformation Program: Year 2 Awards (CMS Fact Sheet, Nov 9, 2026)
sources.note: CMS announced $10B in Year 2 RHTP awards to all 50 states on Nov 9, 2026 (cumulative $20B of the $50B program; $10B/yr FY2026–FY2030; all funds must be expended by Sept 30, 2032). Each state gets a $100M baseline plus a workload portion weighted by rural population, plan content, state policy actions, and implementation progress; the program's stated goals explicitly name community health workers under workforce development and "innovative care models." Washington's Year 2 award is $177.06M, down from $181.26M in Year 1 (HHS release, Nov 9, 2026). Confirms RHTP remains a live national financing vehicle for CHW-bearing care-coordination models, now performance-informed and competitive year to year.

sources.title: Findhelp Selected by Hawai'i Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation to Modernize Community Referrals (PR Newswire, Nov 6, 2026)
sources.note: A state government agency (not a health system) is deploying a statewide closed-loop referral platform with explicit "closed-loop outcome tracking" — following every referral from initiation to confirmed service delivery — across 470+ registered community organizations and 600+ programs. Evidence that closed-loop referral infrastructure is being adopted nationally beyond the health-system buyer set, strengthening the component-level national-availability argument.

sources.title: North Carolina State Health Plan Begins Statewide Rollout of Infina Connect's Care Coordination Platform for 540,000 State-Funded Members (PR Newswire, Nov 10, 2026)
sources.note: A statewide public payer (NC State Health Plan, 750,000 covered lives, 540,000 state-funded members) is deploying Infina Connect's Intelligent Care Coordinator (ICC) closed-loop care-coordination platform across its new Preferred Provider Program, with statewide rollout targeted for Jan 1, 2027. ICC gives primary care a network-tier view, EHR-agnostic clinical document exchange, and tracks whether a referred member was scheduled, seen, and reported back on. The release calls it "one of the largest statewide rollouts of coordinated care technology in the country," extending the closed-loop-referral buyer set from health systems and corrections departments to a state employee health plan — further evidence the referral-tracking infrastructure is national and in production at payer scale.

claims.claim: Multimodal, native-language patient intake (voice, SMS, text, handwritten notes — in the patient's language) is nationally applicable for US rural healthcare access.
claims.summary: Overall verdict: **PARTIALLY SUPPORTED**. The evidence strongly supports the need for language- and modality-flexible intake in rural care, and federal policy already requires meaningful language access for LEP patients. What is missing is a widely deployed, end-to-end national standard or reimbursement pathway for multimodal intake across voice, SMS, text, paper/handwritten capture, and patient-preferred language.

rationale.label: (a) Does evidence show language/modality barriers block rural care access?
rationale.text:
[SUPPORTED] National evidence shows LEP is associated with worse access to care, less preventive care, and more difficulty obtaining a usual source of care. Rural access literature also explicitly names limited English fluency and low health literacy as barriers to timely care, and rural health-literacy work shows plain-language and telephone outreach can improve screening participation. Taken together, the evidence supports the premise that multimodal, native-language intake is addressing a real rural access barrier rather than a niche convenience.

Strongest sources:
1. Access to Care Among Adults with Limited English Proficiency — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9971409/
2. Healthcare Access in Rural Communities Overview - Rural Health Information Hub — https://www.ruralhealthinfo.org/topics/healthcare-access
3. Health Literacy Research in Rural Areas — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8590389/

rationale.label: (b) Are there existing national programs/products doing this?
rationale.text:
[PARTIALLY SUPPORTED] There are clear national policy frameworks and a growing product ecosystem, but the market is still fragmented. HHS/CMS policy requires language access and telehealth guidance contemplates non-English-speaking patients, while national platforms like CareMessage support bidirectional multilingual texting and vendors such as Sunoh.ai advertise multilingual voice-based documentation. However, the evidence base points more to point solutions and partial workflows than to a standardized national multimodal intake stack that works across modalities and rural settings.

Strongest sources:
1. Section 1557: Ensuring Meaningful Access for Individuals with Limited English Proficiency | HHS.gov — https://www.hhs.gov/civil-rights/for-individuals/section-1557/fs-limited-english-proficiency/index.html
2. TELEHEALTH FOR PROVIDERS: WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW — https://www.cms.gov/files/document/telehealth-toolkit-providers.pdf
3. Using Bi-Directional Text Messaging to Engage Patients | CareMessage — https://www.caremessage.org/using-bi-directional-text-messaging-to-engage-patients/

rationale.label: (c) Do policies/mandates support it?
rationale.text:
[SUPPORTED] Section 1557, CLAS, Title VI/Section 504-linked Medicaid language access obligations, and CMS/CHIPRA reimbursement pathways all support language access and translation/interpretation services. The policy direction is clear: covered entities must provide meaningful access, plain-language information, notices in top languages, and no-cost language assistance; Medicaid states may reimburse interpretation costs and can claim enhanced match in some cases. HHS also says many Medicare telehealth flexibilities run through December 31, 2027, including home-based non-behavioral telehealth, no geographic restrictions for non-behavioral services, audio-only for non-behavioral services, and FQHC/RHC distant-site participation. The SPEAK Act (signed February 3, 2026, in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026) adds a new statutory layer: HHS must publish telehealth language-access guidance by February 2027, covering interpreter integration across the telehealth visit — the first federal statute squarely aimed at language access in telehealth. These policies do not mandate the exact multimodal intake architecture Mi Salud uses, but they do strongly support the underlying practice.

Strongest sources:
1. Translation and Interpretation Services | Medicaid — https://www.medicaid.gov/medicaid/financial-management/medicaid-administrative-claiming/translation-and-interpretation-services
2. CLAS Standards - Think Cultural Health — https://thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/clas/standards
3. Enrollment and Access Barriers for People with Limited English Proficiency — https://www.macpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/Enrollment-and-Access-Barriers-for-People-with-Limited-English-Proficiency.pdf
4. Telehealth policy updates | Telehealth.HHS.gov — https://telehealth.hhs.gov/providers/telehealth-policy/telehealth-policy-updates

rationale.label: (d) What is the national gap?
rationale.text:
[SUPPORTED] The gap is not whether language access is needed; it is that rural health systems lack a broadly adopted, reimbursed, interoperable multimodal intake pathway in the patient’s language. MACPAC and CMS describe language access obligations and reimbursement options, but implementation varies by state and provider, and rural broadband/workforce constraints make video-only or portal-only approaches brittle. Nationally, the market offers pieces of the workflow—texting, interpretation, multilingual documentation—but not a universal, low-bandwidth, low-literacy, language-concordant intake standard.

Strongest sources:
1. Enrollment and Access Barriers for People with Limited English Proficiency — https://www.macpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/Enrollment-and-Access-Barriers-for-People-with-Limited-English-Proficiency.pdf
2. TELEHEALTH FOR PROVIDERS: WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW — https://www.cms.gov/files/document/telehealth-toolkit-providers.pdf
3. Healthcare Access in Rural Communities Overview - Rural Health Information Hub — https://www.ruralhealthinfo.org/topics/healthcare-access

sources.title: Section 1557: Ensuring Meaningful Access for Individuals with Limited English Proficiency | HHS.gov
sources.note: HHS says covered entities must take reasonable steps to provide meaningful access for individuals with LEP, including oral language assistance or written translation, and post notices/taglines in the top 15 state languages.

sources.title: CLAS Standards - Think Cultural Health
sources.note: HHS CLAS standards explicitly call for language assistance at no cost, understandable materials, and services responsive to digital, cultural, language, and health-literacy needs.

sources.title: Translation and Interpretation Services | Medicaid
sources.note: CMS/Medicaid policy says providers must make language services available, states may claim reimbursement for interpretation costs, and CHIPRA can raise the federal match for certain translation/interpretation activities.

sources.title: TELEHEALTH FOR PROVIDERS: WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW
sources.note: CMS telehealth guidance explicitly discusses non-English-speaking patients and rural populations, and instructs providers to plan workflows that support interpreter use and access barriers.

sources.title: Telehealth policy updates | Telehealth.HHS.gov
sources.note: HHS says many Medicare telehealth flexibilities are extended through December 31, 2027, including home-based non-behavioral telehealth, no geographic restrictions for non-behavioral services, audio-only for non-behavioral services, and FQHC/RHC distant-site participation.

sources.title: SPEAK Act telehealth language-access guidance requirement (Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026; analysis: Big Language / Martti)
sources.note: The SPEAK Act, signed February 3, 2026 as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, directs HHS to establish a task force and publish telehealth language- access guidance (interpreter integration before/during/after visits) by February 2027. First federal statute squarely addressing telehealth language access — raises the policy floor for language-concordant virtual intake nationally.

sources.title: Healthcare Access in Rural Communities Overview - Rural Health Information Hub
sources.note: RHIH states rural residents face barriers including transportation, workforce shortages, and confidence communicating with providers, especially when they are not fluent in English or have limited health literacy.

sources.title: Access to Care Among Adults with Limited English Proficiency - PMC
sources.note: National survey analysis found adults with LEP were much more likely to lack a usual source of care and miss preventive services; the study reports 25.6 million LEP individuals in the US.

sources.title: Overview of Health Coverage and Care for Individuals with Limited English Proficiency (LEP) | KFF
sources.note: KFF reports 25.7 million LEP people in the US in 2021, with LEP people three times as likely to be uninsured and disproportionately concentrated among Hispanic and Asian populations.

sources.title: Enrollment and Access Barriers for People with Limited English Proficiency
sources.note: MACPAC summarizes that LEP is linked to worse access and health outcomes, that Medicaid agencies must provide meaningful access, and that the 2024 Section 1557 final rule requires top-15-language notices and accessible communications.

sources.title: A Systematic Review of the Impact of Patient-Physician Non-English Language Concordance on Quality of Care and Outcomes - PubMed
sources.note: Systematic review found that in the majority of situations, language-concordant care improves outcomes; 25 of 33 studies favored language-concordant care on at least one outcome.

sources.title: Health Literacy Research in Rural Areas - PMC
sources.note: Rural-focused literature notes rural adults tend to have lower literacy and that plain-language outreach plus telephone follow-up can improve screening and participation.

sources.title: Using Bi-Directional Text Messaging to Engage Patients | CareMessage
sources.note: CareMessage is a national patient-engagement platform built around texting, with bilingual/bidirectional messaging support and evidence-generation partnerships with FQHCs.

sources.title: Multilingual Scribe Sunoh.ai Drastically Reduces Physician Burnout
sources.note: Vendor case material shows multilingual AI documentation/scribe support already exists in clinical workflows, including Spanish-dialect handling, but it is documentation-focused rather than full intake.

claims.claim: BYOD (bring-your-own-device) remote patient monitoring is nationally applicable for U.S. rural populations.
claims.summary: BYOD RPM is nationally feasible and increasingly practical, but it is not uniformly universal across rural America. The policy and vendor stack is real: Medicare reimburses RPM/RTM, HHS recognizes asynchronous/store-and-forward telehealth, and vendors already ship cellular or app-based RPM workflows nationally. The limiting factors are access, not concept: smartphone ownership is high but not universal, seniors lag, rural broadband is still weaker than suburban access, and some rural patients will need cellular gateways or store-and-forward workflows rather than app-only designs.

rationale.label: (a) Smartphone / smartwatch ownership, including rural and seniors
rationale.text:
[PARTIALLY SUPPORTED] **Rationale:** Pew shows the device base is large enough to make BYOD RPM workable nationally: 91% of U.S. adults own smartphones, and 37% own smartwatches. But adoption drops for older adults (79% smartphone ownership and 24% smartwatch ownership for age 65+), and Pew continues to note that rural adults are less likely than urban adults to own smartphones and less likely than suburban adults to have home broadband. So the demographic base is strong, but BYOD cannot assume every rural or older patient already has the needed device stack.

**3 strongest sources:**
1. Pew mobile fact sheet — 91% smartphone ownership; 79% among adults 65+
2. Pew 2024 mobile technology/home broadband report — rural broadband and smartphone-dependent gaps
3. Pew smartwatch charts — 37% overall; 24% for age 65+

rationale.label: (b) National RPM reimbursement landscape
rationale.text:
[SUPPORTED] **Rationale:** CMS clearly covers remote patient monitoring in Medicare and breaks it into setup, device supply, and treatment-management components. CMS also states the same payment logic applies regardless of the specific device type, and the agency’s MLN guidance ties RPM/RTM to secure electronic transmission, consent, and day-count rules. RTM is also a standing Medicare code family, so nationally there is a reimbursement pathway for both physiologic RPM and therapeutic monitoring. The CY2026 PFS final rule adds short-duration codes 99445 and 99470 (effective Jan 1, 2026), so a rural practice can now bill for monitoring periods as short as 2 days and management under 20 minutes — directly easing the ramp-up burden for low-volume rural RPM programs. The CY2027 PFS final rule (CMS-1848-F, issued Nov 4, 2026, effective Jan 1, 2027) finalized tightening of the remote-monitoring rules — a separately reportable face-to-face initiating visit (in person or by telehealth) is now required before RPM/RTM onset, and RTM is limited to established patients; both are conditions of payment. CMS also finalized practice-expense reductions to the device-supply/setup codes (99445, 99453, 99454, 98975–98977, 98984, 98985), phased in at no more than 19%/year, while leaving the treatment-management codes uncut, and did not adopt the floated consolidation of the 17 RPM/RTM codes into 4 G-codes. Critically for community-based and CHW-staffed monitoring models, the proposed direct-employee clinical-staff requirement was finalized but delayed to Jan 1, 2029, so third-party staffing remains permitted through Dec 31, 2028. The reimbursement pathway itself remains intact; the 2029 staffing deadline is the key structural watch item, and the new initiating-visit requirement is a modest ramp-up step (satisfiable by an existing visit, and by telehealth through 12/31/2027).

**3 strongest sources:**
1. CMS Remote Patient Monitoring page — Medicare broadly covers RPM and defines the core components

rationale.label: (c) Existing BYOD-compatible RPM platforms and home diagnostic kits nationally
rationale.text:
[SUPPORTED] **Rationale:** There are already national vendors built for low-friction monitoring. Tenovi is the clearest example: its cellular gateway works with 60+ FDA-cleared devices, needs no app or Wi-Fi, and pushes data over cellular networks. Optimize Health and Healthie also show the broader national platform layer: software plus patient-friendly devices/support, and support for wearable/mobile-app/home-device workflows. That means BYOD-compatible RPM is not hypothetical; it is already a commercial category.

**3 strongest sources:**
1. Tenovi Gateway page — 60+ devices, no app, no Wi-Fi, cellular transmission
2. Optimize Health remote healthcare page — RPM software with patient-friendly devices and support
3. Healthie remote monitoring glossary — wearable devices, mobile apps, and home-based monitoring devices

rationale.label: (d) Broadband constraints in rural U.S. and store-and-forward as a solution
rationale.text:
[PARTIALLY SUPPORTED] **Rationale:** Rural connectivity is a real constraint. Pew reports rural adults trail suburban adults on home broadband, and FCC’s 2024 broadband reporting shows the federal benchmark gap is still meaningful in rural areas. Store-and-forward is a recognized telehealth modality: HHS explicitly defines asynchronous telehealth as store-and-forward and lists text, images, and report uploads as valid workflows. However, it is only a partial solution for RPM because Medicare’s normal telehealth rules are still largely synchronous, and CMS’s explicit store-and-forward billing example is narrow (G2010, largely tied to specific circumstances rather than a universal RPM workaround).

**3 strongest sources:**
1. FCC Internet Access Services: Status as of June 30, 2024 — national broadband baseline
2. HHS asynchronous telehealth guide — store-and-forward recognized as a telehealth modality
3. CMS telemedicine fact sheet — G2010 store-and-forward is recognized but limited

rationale.label: (e) The national gap
rationale.text:
[SUPPORTED] **Rationale:** The gap is not whether RPM exists nationally; it does. The gap is that universal national applicability requires design choices to bridge uneven device ownership, older-adult adoption, and rural broadband constraints. That is exactly where BYOD plus cellular gateways plus store-and-forward can fill the need: it reduces hardware procurement burden and makes deployment possible in lower-bandwidth communities. The remaining gap is operational, not conceptual—patient onboarding, data transport, and reimbursement alignment still need to be configured to local access realities.

**3 strongest sources:**
1. Pew smartphone and broadband reports — high overall adoption but rural/older gaps remain
2. CMS RPM/RTM guidance — reimbursement is available, but only under defined rules
3. Tenovi / Healthie / Optimize Health — the market already supports low-friction and BYOD-friendly workflows

sources.title: Americans’ Use of Mobile Devices in 2026 | Pew Research Center
sources.note: Pew’s Oct 19, 2026 mobile fact sheet (NPORS, fielded Jan 30–Jun 18, 2026) reports 91% of U.S. adults own a smartphone and 98% own a cellphone. It shows a steep age gradient: 79% of adults 65+ own a smartphone while 14% have a cellphone but not a smartphone.

sources.title: Americans’ Use of Mobile Technology and Home Broadband | Pew Research Center
sources.note: Pew reports 90% smartphone ownership and 80% home broadband in 2023, with rural adults at 73% home broadband and 15% of adults being smartphone-dependent. It is the clearest single source for community-type digital gaps.

sources.title: Some digital divides between rural, urban and suburban America | Pew Research Center
sources.note: Pew states rural adults remain less likely than suburban adults to have home broadband and less likely than urban adults to own a smartphone, tablet, or traditional computer. This supports the rural access gap even where nationwide adoption is high.

sources.title: About 4 in 10 U.S. adults have a smartwatch | Pew Research Center
sources.note: Pew’s 2026 chart says 37% of U.S. adults have a smartwatch. A companion chart shows 24% adoption among adults 65+, confirming that smartwatch BYOD is useful but not universal.

sources.title: Just under half of adults under 50 have a smartwatch, while smaller shares of older adults say so | Pew Research Center
sources.note: Pew breaks smartwatch ownership out by age: 44% for ages 18-29, 44% for ages 30-49, 35% for ages 50-64, and 24% for 65+. This underscores the older-adult adoption gap relevant to rural RPM.

sources.title: Calendar Year (CY) 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule Fact Sheet (CMS-1832-F)
sources.note: Finalized Oct 31, 2025, effective Jan 1, 2026: CMS added short-duration RPM codes CPT 99445 (physiologic monitoring over 2–15 days in a 30-day period, ~$47, equal valuation to 99454) and CPT 99470 (first 10 minutes of treatment management, ~$26, requires one real-time interaction), lowering the practical billing floor for RPM starts; existing RPM/RTM code set unchanged. Code detail per HumHealth analysis (https://www.humhealth.com/blog/new-remote-patient-monitoring-cpt-codes-2026/).

sources.title: Calendar Year (CY) 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule Fact Sheet (CMS-1848-F)
sources.note: Final rule issued Nov 4, 2026 (public inspection; published Nov 9; effective Jan 1, 2027): CMS finalized three of the four proposed RPM/RTM policies — (1) RTM limited to established patients, (2) a separately reportable face-to-face initiating visit (in person or telehealth) required before RPM or RTM onset, and (3) practice-expense revaluation of device-supply/setup codes (CPT 99445, 99453, 99454, 98975–98977, 98984, 98985), capped at 19%/yr so the cuts phase in over two years; the treatment-management codes (99457, 99458, 99470, 98979–98981) were NOT cut. The proposed direct-employee clinical-staff requirement was finalized but DELAYED two years to Jan 1, 2029 (third-party contracting remains allowed through Dec 31, 2028; CMS to issue clarifying sub-regulatory guidance on leased employees/independent contractors). The floated bundling of the 17 RPM/RTM codes into 4 G-codes was NOT adopted. CY2027 non-qualifying-APM conversion factor $32.63 (−2.31%). Detail per Nixon Peabody alert (Nov 9, 2026, nixonpeabody.com).

sources.title: Remote Patient Monitoring | CMS
sources.note: CMS says Medicare broadly covers RPM using connected medical devices that automatically transmit data, with separate setup, device-supply, and management components. CMS also says payment does not depend on the exact type of device used.

sources.title: MLN901705 - Telehealth & Remote Monitoring | CMS
sources.note: CMS explains RPM/RTM rules: remote monitoring includes RPM and RTM, data must be electronically collected and uploaded securely, patient consent is required, and RPM cannot be billed concurrently with RTM for the same monitoring activity.

sources.title: CMS Manual System
sources.note: CMS states the RTM code family includes CPT 98975, 98976, 98977, 98980, and 98981, and that these were designated as sometimes-therapy codes. This confirms RTM is an established national Medicare code path alongside RPM.

sources.title: MEDICARE TELEMEDICINE HEALTH CARE PROVIDER FACT SHEET | CMS
sources.note: CMS defines HCPCS G2010 as remote evaluation of recorded video and/or images submitted by an established patient, explicitly described as store-and-forward, with a follow-up requirement. The fact sheet also reflects that standard Medicare telehealth is otherwise interactive and synchronous.

sources.title: Asynchronous direct-to-consumer telehealth | Telehealth.HHS.gov
sources.note: HHS says asynchronous telehealth is also known as store-and-forward and is often used for intake or follow-up. It specifically recognizes text, image, and report upload workflows as legitimate telehealth patterns.

sources.title: What are different types of telehealth? | Telehealth.HHS.gov
sources.note: HHS lists remote patient monitoring as a standard telehealth type and describes RPM as using tools to collect and share health data from home. This is helpful for framing BYOD RPM as mainstream telehealth rather than a niche workaround.

sources.title: FCC Internet Access Services: Status as of June 30, 2024 | Federal Communications Commission
sources.note: FCC’s June 2024 internet-access report is the official national data source for broadband availability and connection speeds. It provides the underlying federal baseline for evaluating rural connectivity constraints.

sources.title: FCC Releases Adopted 2024 Section 706 Report | TLP Law
sources.note: This summary of the FCC’s 2024 report quotes rural access figures of 83.1% at 25/3 Mbps and 72% at 100/20 Mbps. I used it to capture the rural-specific figures in readable form.

sources.title: Tenovi Gateway - Cellular Connectivity for 60+ RPM Devices | Tenovi
sources.note: Tenovi says its cellular gateway connects to 60+ FDA-cleared RPM and RTM devices, requires no app or Wi-Fi, and sends data over cellular networks. This is a strong example of a national BYOD-lite / low-friction RPM kit model.

sources.title: Remote Healthcare - Optimize Health | Optimize Health
sources.note: Optimize Health markets remote patient monitoring software plus patient-friendly devices and support. It supports the broader claim that nationally distributed RPM vendors already package software, device logistics, and support together.

sources.title: Benefits of Remote Patient Monitoring | Healthie
sources.note: Healthie says remote monitoring can use wearable devices, mobile apps, and home-based monitoring devices, and that data are transmitted to clinicians for decision-making. This is evidence of a platform layer that can support BYOD workflows.
